name: Stealth automation — the toolchain that patches an automated browser to look unautomated. Principal members: puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth (Node, the original), playwright-stealth / tf-playwright-stealth (Python ports of the same evasion set), undetected-chromedriver (Python, patched ChromeDriver binary), SeleniumBase UC/CDP Mode, nodriver (the author's successor to undetected-chromedriver), rebrowser-patches, and Camoufox (a compiled Firefox fork). Also called 'anti-detect' or 'evasion' tooling.
kind: Libraries and, in Camoufox's case, a browser build. Not standards, not benchmarks. The detection counterparts they are measured against (CreepJS, Scrapfly's automation detector, deviceandbrowserinfo probes, and the commercial bundles themselves) are the closest thing this area has to a benchmark suite.
maturity: Sharply bifurcated. The JS-injection generation is effectively deprecated: puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth has had no significant maintenance since 2023 and is now widely described as not viable at scale; playwright-stealth inherits the same evasion list and the same decay; undetected-chromedriver still defeats naive checks but its specific patches have been catalogued by vendors, and its own author moved on to nodriver. The current generation is architecturally different — nodriver and SeleniumBase CDP Mode avoid the detectable protocol commands rather than patching their symptoms, and Camoufox compiles the spoofing into Firefox's C++ so there is no JavaScript patch to observe at all. Camoufox is the only member of this family that is architecturally relevant to a Firefox-driving project, and it is actively maintained.
license: puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth: MIT. undetected-chromedriver: GPL-3.0 — a real consideration, since GPL-3.0 is copyleft and linking it into a distributed system carries obligations. playwright-stealth: MIT/Apache-family [uncertain]. nodriver: AGPL-3.0 in its published form [uncertain], which would be a serious constraint on any distributed use. Camoufox: MPL-2.0, inherited from Firefox, which permits use. For this project the licensing question is moot for everything except Camoufox, which is permissively enough licensed to adopt if the project ever decided to — a decision this item argues against on other grounds.
keeps_and_discards: These tools extract nothing and discard nothing from the page; they operate entirely on the environment the page observes. The JS-injection generation replaces or wraps a specific list of surfaces: navigator.webdriver, navigator.plugins and mimeTypes, navigator.languages, window.chrome, Permissions.query, WebGL getParameter's vendor and renderer strings, iframe.contentWindow, the User-Agent and its Client Hints, and media codec support. undetected-chromedriver additionally rewrites the ChromeDriver binary to rename the cdc_ prefixed variables it injects into the page. Camoufox replaces the same conceptual set but does it in the engine, so what the page reads is what the engine genuinely returns. In every case the page's content is untouched — the value proposition is purely 'the page serves you the real document instead of a challenge', which is a gating effect, not an extraction effect.
structure_preserved: Fully — no DOM transformation occurs. The one structural side effect worth stating is positive and is the entire reason anyone uses these: on an anti-bot-fronted origin, an undetected session yields the real document tree while a detected session yields a challenge stub, so structure preservation here is binary and upstream. Shadow boundaries are untouched by every member of the family; none of them patches attachShadow, and that absence is itself evidence about the target set (see mechanism_detectability).
interactive_elements: Untouched as content. The relevant handling is on the actuator side: several members add humanised interaction — nodriver and Camoufox offer human-like cursor trajectories and typing cadence, and Camoufox exposes a humanised-cursor movement option — because behavioural uniformity is now a larger share of detection than static fingerprint. This is the part of the family with the clearest transfer to this project, and also the part that most directly conflicts with an O(delta) sensor's need for fast, deterministic actuation: human-like actuation is slow and stochastic by construction.
interactive_state_fidelity: No direct effect — disabled / checked / selected / expanded and the ARIA layer are all page-authored and untouched. The indirect effect is large and runs the right way: a detected session frequently receives a page that never fully hydrates, freezing ARIA state at parse-time values, so stealth that avoids detection preserves state fidelity by preserving hydration. That is the honest case for this family in extraction terms: it does not improve the representation, it prevents the representation from being of the wrong document. The token cost is zero.
layout_awareness: The tools read and spoof window-level geometry — screen dimensions, availWidth/availHeight, devicePixelRatio, outerWidth/outerHeight and the outer-minus-inner delta that betrays headless — because those are fingerprint attributes and, in headless-default form, blatant ones. This is geometry as an actuator configuration property, read once at the window level, and it sits exactly where this project's no-layout-in-the-fold constraint says such things belong: in the peripheral, owned by the actuator. Nothing here asks the fold to read per-node geometry.
javascript_required: The JS-injection generation requires script execution by definition — its evasions ARE scripts, and they must be installed before any page script runs (via Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument or Playwright's addInitScript), which creates both a race and an observable. Camoufox requires no injected script for its core spoofing, which is the architectural point. On the reading side, all of them presuppose full page script execution, so telemetry fires normally; nothing in this family reduces what the page's own scripts observe or send.
evaluation_method: Almost entirely by probe-page pass/fail plus anecdotal challenge-rate reporting, and this is the field's central evidentiary weakness. The standard method is: point the tool at CreepJS, Scrapfly's automation detector, bot.sannysoft.com, or a live Cloudflare/DataDome-protected page, and report whether it passes or is challenged. CreepJS is the most rigorous of these and its method is worth naming precisely because it is the one that transfers: its lies module asks the same questions from the main thread, from a Web Worker, and from an iframe — three fresh realms — and treats disagreement between realms as the finding, alongside .toString() output checks, prototype-chain consistency checks, and whether a function throws the TypeError a genuine native implementation would. That cross-realm differential is an oracle-free consistency test, not a heuristic, and it is why single-realm patching fails.
corpus_size_and_origins: There is no corpus. Evaluations are single-probe or few-site, run at one moment, from one egress address, usually by a party selling either the tool or its competitor. Where numbers appear at all they are of the form 'passes CreepJS' or 'bypasses Cloudflare' with no site count, no time window, no repetition, and no control for IP reputation — which adjacent evidence indicates dominates the outcome at scale. One figure recurs and should be treated with suspicion because its provenance is a vendor blog rather than a measurement: that navigator.webdriver as a single signal accounts for under 5% of real-world automation detections in 2026. The claim is plausible in the sense that no serious detector relies on one signal, but the denominator is undefined and the number is unsourced. [uncertain]
reported_precision_recall: None published in any usable form, by anyone, in either direction. Evasion vendors report binary pass/fail against named detectors; detection vendors report nothing quantitative for the reason described in the CDP item — publishing an operating point hands it to the adversary. The most defensible qualitative summary from the current sources: the JS-injection generation reliably defeats naive checks (a bare navigator.webdriver read, bot.sannysoft.com) and reliably fails against Cloudflare Turnstile, DataDome and PerimeterX at their current configurations; the protocol-avoidance generation (nodriver, SeleniumBase CDP Mode) and the compiled generation (Camoufox) fare materially better; and none of them is claimed to be durable, because the equilibrium moves.
independent_oracle: Yes, in two forms, and this family is better served than most. CreepJS's cross-realm differential is a genuine oracle: it does not encode a belief about what a bot looks like, it tests internal consistency, so a perfectly consistent environment passes regardless of what the tester believes. The commercial detectors are a second, opaque oracle with no shared assumptions and a strong commercial incentive to be correct. What is missing is an oracle for the thing that actually matters — whether the CONTENT received differs from what a human would receive — since passing a probe page proves nothing about whether an origin quietly served a reduced dataset.
evidence_independence: Poor. Essentially every quantitative claim in this space originates from a company selling scraping infrastructure (Zenrows, Scrapfly, Sendwin, Bright Data, Scrappey) or from a company selling detection (DataDome, Castle, Kasada). Both sides are motivated to overstate the sophistication of the arms race, which is the one thing they agree on. The open-source tool authors are the most credible sources about their own tools' limitations — undetected-chromedriver's author effectively deprecating it in favour of nodriver, and puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth going unmaintained, are the strongest available signals about the JS-injection generation's viability, and both are self-administered negatives. CreepJS, being an independent research probe with published source and no commercial position, is the single most trustworthy artifact in the item.
page_archetype_coverage: Not measured, and the skew is the same as for CDP detection: heavy anti-bot deployment on e-commerce, ticketing, travel, finance, streaming and job boards; near-zero on documentation, archives, government and academic sites. The practical consequence for this project is that on an archive- and documentation-leaning corpus these tools would purchase nothing, because there is nothing to evade — and on a commercial corpus they would purchase access at the price of the constraint violations catalogued below. A project that reports a single aggregate 'capture success rate' across a mixed corpus is averaging two populations with entirely different mechanics.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Locale is an evasion surface rather than a robustness concern: these tools spoof Accept-Language, timezone and geolocation, and Camoufox spoofs them coherently as a set, which matters because incoherence between them (a US timezone with a Japanese Accept-Language and a European IP) is itself a strong detection signal — coherence, not any single value, is what the consistency-checking detectors test. There is no CJK- or RTL-specific behaviour because no text is processed. One asymmetry worth recording: detection thresholds vary by geography and ASN, so the same tool's apparent effectiveness differs by where it egresses from, and no published evaluation controls for this. [uncertain]
leaks_outward: Two disclosures, one intended and one not. Intended: the spoofed attribute set is disclosed to the page as if genuine, which is the product. Unintended and more consequential: a failed evasion discloses strictly more than no evasion would. An unpatched automated browser says 'I am automated'; a detected stealth browser says 'I am automated AND actively concealing it', which is a categorically worse signal to send to a reputation system that shares data across every site its vendor fronts. Additionally, the specific patch set is itself an identifier — the exact combination of spoofed values a given tool version produces is a stable fingerprint, so using a popular stealth tool places the session in a small, well-catalogued bucket rather than a large anonymous one. This is the anti-detect field's core irony and it is well established: the evasion is the fingerprint.
mechanism_detectability: This is the decisive item for the project's first tension, and it supplies the concrete production evidence the earlier items could only bound. Prototype patching IS detected in production, generically, and the mechanism is public. CreepJS's lies module — 953 lines devoted to exactly this — inspects property descriptors, checks .toString() output against native form, verifies prototype-chain consistency, tests whether a function throws the TypeError a native implementation would, and, most decisively, asks the same questions from the main thread, from a Web Worker, and from an iframe. Each is a fresh realm with a fresh set of native objects; a patch installed in the main realm is simply absent in a new iframe's Element.prototype, and the disagreement is the finding. That check is generic — it does not need to know in advance which method was patched — and equivalent cross-realm and toString-integrity checks are shipped in commercial bundles, which is precisely why puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth now fails against Cloudflare, DataDome and PerimeterX. So: an attachShadow patch WOULD be caught, not by a targeted attachShadow check but by a generic realm-consistency sweep, unless the patcher also hooked every iframe and worker realm at creation — which is itself more machinery, more racing against page scripts, and more surface. The refusal is therefore NOT arbitrary in the way the tension's framing suggests: patching attachShadow is genuinely detectable by mechanisms genuinely deployed today. But the comparison still resolves against the current justification, on a different axis. navigator.webdriver under Marionette is a W3C-specified boolean, set true for the session's lifetime, read first by every commercial bundle, requiring no realm sweep, no timing, and no cleverness — it fires unconditionally on 100% of sessions with certainty 1. attachShadow patching fires conditionally, on origins that run a generic integrity sweep, and only for those that sweep Element.prototype. FINAL SETTLEMENT: both are detectable; the accepted exposure (Marionette) is unconditional and universal, the refused one (attachShadow) is conditional and narrower. Refusing the smaller exposure while accepting the larger is inconsistent if detectability is the sole criterion. The constraint should be retained and re-grounded on the reasons that actually survive scrutiny — honouring an author's explicit encapsulation boundary, avoiding a permanent race against page scripts, avoiding breakage of pages that probe their own roots, and avoiding the maintenance burden of hooking every realm — all of which are sound, none of which depends on relative detectability, and all of which point the same way. A secondary and cleaner resolution is available and preferable: declare agency (Web Bot Auth), at which point neither exposure is a cost and the encapsulation argument stands alone.
countermeasures: Read in reverse here — the countermeasures against these tools are what production deploys, and they are: cross-realm consistency sweeps (CreepJS-style, generic), native-function toString and descriptor integrity checks, coherence checks across the spoofed attribute set (timezone vs locale vs IP geolocation vs WebGL renderer vs font list), behavioural analysis of pointer and keystroke entropy, TLS and HTTP/2 fingerprinting below the browser entirely (JA3/JA4, which no in-browser patch can touch), and IP/ASN reputation. The last two are the reason the arms race has moved off the JavaScript layer: a perfectly spoofed browser egressing from a datacenter ASN over a mismatched TLS fingerprint is caught without any page script running. That is worth internalising, because it means in-browser stealth is now the least important variable, and no amount of it fixes an identity problem.
measured_fidelity_cost: Unmeasured everywhere in the literature, and measurable here. In fold terms the cost of Camoufox-class engine spoofing should be near zero on saved pages — it changes no DOM and blocks no requests, so it belongs in the same class as the fingerprint-hardening arms that stayed inside 2.3x of the 0.07% floor, not in the class of block_trackers' 10.49% live cost, which is request suppression. The cost of humanised actuation is the opposite and is potentially large but is a latency and determinism cost rather than a fidelity cost: stochastic cursor paths and typed cadence make actuation slow and non-reproducible, which collides directly with an O(delta) sensor's need for cheap deterministic steps. The measurement worth running is the one already implied by the corpus setup: fold live anti-bot-fronted origins with and without a stealth-configured driver, and compare fold size and content overlap against the same origins' saved copies. If detected sessions produce order-of-magnitude smaller folds, that number belongs in a gate-state ledger and not in the hardening-cost ledger at all.
gate_state_at_capture: None of these tools records gate state; their entire purpose is to make the gate not happen, which quietly converts a recordable fact into an unrecorded one. That is a real methodological hazard for a corpus: a capture obtained by successful evasion looks identical to a capture from an ungated origin, and the two are not equivalent — the first was obtained by defeating an access control, the second was freely served. Any use of this family must be accompanied by a per-capture record of what evasion was active, or the corpus loses the ability to distinguish the two, which is both a reproducibility problem and, given the legal exposure below, a compliance problem.
determinism: The tools themselves are deterministic in what they spoof, with two exceptions: several randomise fingerprint values per session by design (Camoufox can rotate fingerprints, and undetected-chromedriver randomises the cdc_ variable names it substitutes), and humanised actuation is stochastic by construction. The OUTCOME is not deterministic at all, because it depends on a remote, mutable, reputation-sensitive detector — the same tool against the same site from the same machine can pass and then fail. Any single-run 'it works' observation is uninformative, and the field is nonetheless built almost entirely on single-run observations.
determinism_across_versions: Very poor, on both sides of the equation. Browser updates break evasions (new surfaces appear, old ones change shape); detector updates break them faster and without announcement; and the tools' own versions change what they spoof. Camoufox's engine-level approach is the most durable because it tracks Firefox releases rather than racing page scripts, but it consequently lags Firefox releases and pins the project to a fork's release cadence rather than upstream's — a real operational cost for a project that has already committed to a real-browser, no-mocks stance. The JS-injection generation's decay is now measured in the plainest possible way: it stopped being maintained and stopped working, roughly together.
reproducibility: Weak. Results are not reproducible across time because the detector side is remote and mutable, not reproducible across egress because IP and ASN reputation dominates, and not reproducible across tool versions. No fixed evaluation corpus exists and none could, since the interesting targets are live commercial sites whose behaviour is the variable under test. This is the strongest general argument against building any measured claim on this family: the substrate is not stable enough to support one.
failure_modes: Ranked by how badly they hurt. Worst: silent content degradation, where the evasion partially succeeds, the page serves a reduced or stale dataset, and the fold looks entirely normal. Next: partial-realm patching, where the main frame is spoofed and an iframe or worker is not, producing the cross-realm disagreement CreepJS is built to find — this is the specific failure that an attachShadow patch would exhibit. Next: attribute incoherence, where individually plausible spoofed values are jointly impossible. Next: patch-race loss, where a page script reads a surface before the init script installed the patch. Then binary-signature detection (undetected-chromedriver's catalogued patches). Then the loud, benign case: an outright challenge or 403. Finally, and outside the browser entirely: TLS/JA4 and ASN mismatch, which no member of this family addresses and which is increasingly the deciding factor.
failure_visibility: Silently degrading, which is the anti-pattern this project explicitly refuses, and this family is one of the purest instances of it available. The tools report success when the page loaded; they have no notion of whether the page loaded CORRECTLY, and the detectors are deliberately engineered to prefer invisible degradation over visible challenges precisely so that the adversary cannot tell. Adopting anything from this family without an independent content-correctness control would import exactly the failure mode the project's constraints exist to exclude. The available control is the same one the CDP item identified: cross-identity fold diffing.
scale_limits: Cost per session is small; the binding limit is per-identity and it is reached early. Reputation systems aggregate across sites and over time, so the effective limit is requests-per-identity-per-window rather than anything about the browser, and at 3,082 requests per corpus run to 92+ distinct hosts, this project already operates well past the scale where in-browser stealth is the deciding variable. Beyond that point the only levers are identity diversity (residential proxies, rotating profiles) which brings its own cost, its own legal exposure, and its own ethics — and which converts a technical question into a procurement one.
delta_cost_model: Not applicable — these tools maintain no incremental structure. One negative interaction with the project's O(delta) commitment deserves stating: humanised actuation deliberately injects latency and randomness into every interaction, so an actuator built on it has a per-action cost that is both large and variable. An O(delta) sensor whose actuator is deliberately slowed to look human has traded its central performance property for access, and that trade should be made explicitly if at all rather than inherited from a library default.
reanchoring_stability: No node-identity machinery of any kind. The indirect effect is the same total-substitution pattern noted for CDP detection: an undetected session anchors against the real document, a detected one anchors against a challenge page, and switching between them invalidates every anchor for that URL simultaneously. That simultaneity remains the cheap discriminator between a gate event and ordinary DOM churn, and it needs no knowledge of what these tools do.
adversarial_exposure: This family preserves no content and filters none, so it neither adds nor removes invisible-content exposure. Its contribution to the second tension is a caution about the threat model's shape: it demonstrates concretely that what a page serves is a function of who the page thinks is reading, which means single-capture concealment analysis — Unicode, DOM, geometric or otherwise — has a hard ceiling no filter can raise. A page that serves clean content to a suspected agent and injected content to an apparent human, or the reverse, is undetectable from one capture by any means. This strengthens the case that cross-identity comparison is not an optional refinement but the only available detector for an entire concealment class, and it is one a layout-blind fold can perform as well as any other.
provenance_carrying: None. What this item requires of the project's provenance is one more peripheral field: the driver configuration and evasion state under which a capture was taken. Without it, a corpus assembled over months across changing driver settings is uninterpretable, because the single largest determinant of what was served is not recorded anywhere. This is cheap to add and belongs beside egress class and gate state, outside the fold.
roundtrip_safety: Not applicable — nothing is serialised, no escaping policy exists. The only adjacent observation is that challenge and interstitial pages, which are what a failed evasion yields, contain heavily obfuscated inline script that will roundtrip perfectly while carrying no information, again illustrating that roundtrip stability is necessary and not sufficient as a fidelity oracle.
token_budget_and_ordering: No effect on ordering or truncation. The budget-relevant consequence is upstream and binary: an evaded page costs a full page's tokens and delivers a full page's information; a detected page costs a small number of tokens and delivers none, or — the expensive case — costs a full page's tokens for a partially-hydrated skeleton with a terrible information-per-token ratio. If any gate or degradation state is known, it must be surfaced early in whatever the SLM receives, not left to be inferred from the content, because a plausible-looking skeleton gives the model no cue at all.
representation_cost: Zero for the tooling itself. The real costs are elsewhere: latency (humanised actuation), operational (tracking a browser fork's release cadence, in Camoufox's case), legal (see below), and reputational — a detected evasion is a worse signal to a shared reputation system than no evasion at all, and that cost is borne across every origin the vendor fronts, not just the one where detection occurred.
what_could_be_adopted: Very little as code, three things as method. (1) CreepJS's cross-realm differential — asking the same question from the main thread, a worker and a fresh iframe and treating disagreement as the finding — is a genuinely oracle-free consistency test and generalises far beyond fingerprinting; the project should adopt the pattern for its own self-checks, and it is also the correct way to verify that no unintended patching is present. (2) The coherence principle: a set of individually plausible values that are jointly impossible is the detectable thing, which argues that partial hardening is worse than none, and applies directly to the project's own hardening-arm design. (3) Camoufox's architectural lesson stated as a negative — the only way to spoof without a detectable patch is to change the engine, which is a far heavier commitment than patching and one this project should decline. Concretely, the recommendation is to adopt none of these tools, keep Marionette with navigator.webdriver true, record it as a peripheral field, and accept differentiated service as recorded data rather than as a problem to defeat.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS (vacuously — no page structure is read or classified). no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE IN THE ACTUATOR LAYER ONLY — window-level geometry spoofing is real and necessary if the family is used at all, but it is window configuration owned by the actuator, never per-node geometry entering the fold. o_delta: NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY — humanised actuation deliberately trades latency and determinism for realism, which is the opposite of the project's performance commitment; adopting it would silently forfeit the O(delta) property at the actuator boundary. no_mocks: REJECTED, and this is the sharpest conflict in the item — the entire family exists to present a false environment to the page, which is the definition of a mock, merely pointed outward rather than inward. A project whose no-mocks constraint means 'real browser, real embedder, no stubs in any measured path' cannot coherently install a layer whose purpose is to make the browser report values it does not have. The constraint as written targets internal stubs, but the spirit plainly extends here, and stealth tooling should be rejected on this ground alone, independently of detectability. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY, and the item's central evidentiary contribution — CreepJS's generic cross-realm and toString-integrity sweep, and its commercial equivalents, would catch an attachShadow patch without needing to target it, which confirms the refusal is substantively correct rather than arbitrary; but the same evidence shows navigator.webdriver under Marionette is an unconditional, universally-read exposure of greater certainty, so the two positions cannot both be justified by detectability alone. Retain the constraint, re-ground it on encapsulation and stability, and resolve the Marionette exposure by declaring agency rather than by concealing it. Overall verdict: REJECTED as an adoptable technology, valuable as a negative oracle and as a source of one reusable test pattern.
governance_signal_handling: Diametrically opposed to the governance stack and this is the cleanest way to see why the stack exists. Stealth tooling ignores robots.txt, Content Signals, ai.txt and AIPREF by construction — its premise is that the site's expressed preference about automated access should be circumvented rather than read. Web Bot Auth is its exact inverse: cryptographically declare that you are an agent and accept whatever service that entitles you to. HTTP 402 pay-per-crawl is the economic form of the same inversion. A project that reads governance signals in one breath and evades detection in the next is incoherent, and the incoherence is not merely aesthetic — an origin that publishes an AIPREF policy and also deploys DataDome has expressed its preference twice, and evading the second while reading the first is choosing which of the site's own statements to honour. The consistent positions are: declare and comply, or do neither. This project's other commitments point unambiguously at the first.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: The most exposed item in this research set. Evading a technical access-control measure is legally distinct from scraping a freely-served page: hiQ v. LinkedIn narrowed CFAA exposure for public data but explicitly did not authorise circumventing technical barriers, and the subsequent proceedings went against hiQ on contract grounds; EU member-state implementations of the Cybercrime Convention treat circumvention of access controls as an offence largely independent of the data's public nature; and terms-of-service breach is near-certain wherever an anti-bot product is deployed, since deploying one is an unambiguous expression of non-consent. Under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026, where persistent storage of scraped content is the regulated act and legitimate interest requires a balancing test, content acquired by defeating an access control is materially harder to defend in that balancing — the data subject's and the publisher's reasonable expectations are precisely what the control expresses. On PII, these tools retain nothing themselves, but they enable capture of gated content that is disproportionately more likely to contain personal data (logged-in views, member directories, user-generated commercial content) than the open pages they would otherwise reach. The defensible posture is to not adopt this family, to record 'challenged' as a terminal gate state, and to let the corpus carry an honest gap.
